To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Mendelian randomization does no support serum calcium in overall or advanced prostate risk.
we did not find evidence that serum calcium increases prostate cancer risk.
we found weak evidence for an effect on prostate cancer risk, and no evidence for an effect in men with advanced prostate cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the causal effect of serum calcium levels on risk of prostate, and advanced prostate, cancer.
the relationship between serum calcium and the risk of prostate cancer, which has been the subject of a number of epidemiological studies.
the role of genetic factors on prostate cancer risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Mendelian randomization results are consistent with no causal effect of serum calcium levels on prostate cancer risk.

the evidence for an association between serum calcium and prostate cancer risk is inconclusive, but does not support the notion that a 0.50 mg/dL (1 SD) increase in serum calcium is associated to an increased risk of prostate cancer.
Mendelian randomization does support the observational evidence for a protective association of calcium with prostate cancer risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence for an association of serum calcium with prostate cancer is weak.
there is little evidence to support a causal role of serum calcium in prostate carcinogenesis, although residual confounding may have led to an underestimate of the true effect.
Mendelian randomization does NOT support a causal role for serum calcium in prostate risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Mendelian randomization can help to resolve causal inference in observational data, even when the genetic instrument has low precision (as was the case here).
Mendelian randomization, when applied appropriately, can strengthen causal inferences in observational studies.
the observational evidence linking serum calcium and prostate cancer risk is probably due to residual confounding.
